strengths: Novel perspective: The backward rectification approach using chains of lightweight mapping networks is an interesting and relatively unexplored direction for continual learning

Efficient architecture: Rectifier units exhibit linear parameter growth with careful design (linear compress/combine layers, minimal weak feature extractor), better than TAMiL and CLS-ER for comparable performance

Comprehensive evaluation: Multiple benchmarks (CIFAR10/100, Tiny ImageNet), numerous baselines, ablation studies, and visualization (PCA in Figure 3) showing rectified representations align with targets
Flexible alignment strategy: Framework supports multiple options (task t-1 data, current task data, generative models), providing practical flexibility for different constraints
Honest limitations discussion: Paper acknowledges key limitations including inference overhead of long chains and optimal dependence on task t-1 data
weaknesses: Data requirement contradiction: Achieves best performance (82.05% CIFAR100) with 5000 task t-1 samples, dropping to 69.22% with only current task data. Claims of being 'data-free' or 'strictly data-free' are misleading—the method fundamentally requires task t-1 data retention, making it conceptually similar to rehearsal methods, undermining a core claimed advantage

Unfair experimental comparisons: Main results (Table 1) compare ILR with 5000-sample alignment sets against rehearsal methods with 500-1000 sample buffers. Fair comparison shows ILR-500 (86.28%) underperforms ER-500 (94.24%) on CIFAR10. Paper acknowledges but doesn't remedy this unfairness in primary results

Inference cost completely unaddressed: Task-incremental inference requires sequential passes through N-t rectifiers, but no inference time measurements are provided. Computational overhead remains unquantified despite being a fundamental practical concern. Solution of 'skipping' is deferred to future work

Weak class-incremental solution: Class-incremental performance (Table 2: 48.90%) underperforms CLS-ER baseline (51.13%) with same data. Ensemble averaging approach is acknowledged as problematic for confident classifiers. Class-incremental setting represents major CL scenario but remains incompletely solved

Limited technical novelty: Loss function (Eq. 1) is standard L2+cosine distance combination; rectifier architecture uses simple linear layers with minimal weak feature extractor. Main contribution is framework design rather than novel technical components

Weak feature extractor lacks justification: Extremely simple architecture (2 conv layers, hardcoded to 16×16 input) with no ablation on distillation approach. Generalization to different input sizes, architectures, or domains is unclear. Design appears overfit to CIFAR/ImageNet
Hyperparameter sensitivity: Ablation (Table 5) shows 9.6% drop when τ=0 (82.05%→72.45%), indicating method requires careful tuning with no guidance for new domains

Generative model component underdeveloped: ILR-GAN mentioned but only one result (79.51% vs 82.05% with data). BigGAN training adds computational overhead not discussed. Integration feels like afterthought rather than core contribution

Task diversity assumptions unexplored: No analysis of how rectification performs on truly unrelated sequential tasks or task sequences with distribution shifts. Assumes task similarity without validation

Limited experimental scope: Only vision classification with ResNet18. Generalization to other architectures, tasks, or domains entirely unaddressed. Claims of novelty should be supported by broader evaluation

strengths: Novel perspective on backward rectification for continual learning that provides an alternative to replay buffers and regularization
Solid experimental methodology with comprehensive setup, proper train/val/test splits, and detailed appendices
Effective visualization of the rectification mechanism using PCA (Figure 3), demonstrating that learned mappings recover target representations
Honest discussion of limitations including inference cost, data dependencies, and class-incremental weaknesses
Lightweight rectifier architecture that grows linearly with tasks rather than quadratically
weaknesses: Misleading core positioning: framed as 'data-free' but requires either keeping task t-1 data, storing f_{t-1} representations, or training generative models—fundamentally similar memory requirements to rehearsal methods

Unfair empirical comparisons: ILR-5000 (94.84% on S-CIFAR10) is compared against baselines with 500-1000 buffer samples, but actually underperforms ER-1000 (95.25%) and CLS-ER-1000 (96.05%) under equal memory budgets
Unresolved scalability issues: inference requires sequential processing through N-1 rectifier chains; acknowledged as 'costly' for long sequences but only vague suggestions for solutions

Rectifier architecture choices lack justification: arbitrary design decisions (downsampling to 16×16, distilling h_t from f_{t-1}, specific layer configuration) not empirically validated through ablation
Limited technical novelty: core contribution is learning simple MLPs for representation mapping; lacks theoretical analysis of why backward rectification should be superior to existing approaches
Weak class-incremental learning: degraded performance (71.07%→48.90%) with expensive ensemble inference over all task domains, defeating efficiency claims in the harder problem setting
Marginal parameter efficiency gains: 21.96M (ILR-20 tasks) only slightly better than 23.85M (TAMiL), and comparison ignores actual data storage costs

Incomplete experimental evidence: limited to small-scale image classification, sequential task ordering, and CIFAR/Tiny-ImageNet; no timing comparisons, permuted task sequences, or long-horizon experiments

strengths: Novel direction in continual learning using lightweight rectifier units to correct representation drift, distinct from replay-based, regularization-based, and architecture-expansion approaches
Modular framework that doesn't modify the main training procedure, enabling easy integration into existing pipelines

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmarks with comparisons to diverse representative methods (ER, DER++, ER-ACE, CLS-ER, TAMiL, etc.) including ablations and parameter growth analysis
Strong empirical results on CIFAR100 (82.05%) and Tiny ImageNet (72.50%) with 5000-sample alignment sets, outperforming most baselines
Efficient memory footprint with ~0.5M parameters per task, linear growth compared to TAMiL and CLS-ER
Flexible alignment set options (task t-1 data, task t data, generative models) providing adaptability for different scenarios including privacy-constrained settings
Insightful visualizations (PCA in Figure 3) validating that rectifiers effectively recover target representations
Honest acknowledgment of limitations including inference cost concerns, class-incremental learning challenges, and data requirements
weaknesses: Substantial data requirements contradicting 'data-free' claims: best performance requires 5000 task t-1 samples; with 500 samples, ILR (74.59%) falls below baselines like CLS-ER (77.03%); with equal 1000-sample budgets, ILR (78.53%) underperforms CLS-ER (79.36%), raising fairness concerns in experimental comparisons

Critical inference cost concerns unaddressed: no timing comparisons provided despite acknowledged computational overhead; with 20 tasks requiring 20 rectifier passes, scalability is questionable; proposed 'skipping' solution mentioned but never evaluated

Severe class-incremental learning performance degradation: 48.90% on CIFAR100 vs 82.05% for task-incremental (33% drop); ad-hoc ensemble averaging solution lacks principled approach and remains insufficient

Weak theoretical justification: no formal analysis of why rectification works; alignment loss design (L2 + cosine) lacks theoretical motivation beyond intuition; no characterization of success conditions
Incomplete technical details: distillation of weak feature extractor ht is poorly explained; role of temporary layer gt in training unclear; these gaps impact reproducibility and understanding
Limited scope and generalization: only image classification with ResNet18; no experiments on other domains (NLP, RL); unclear applicability beyond vision tasks
Claimed distinction from network expansion (Section 3.2.2) unconvincing: rectifiers are network expansion by nature; comparison baseline achieving 53% is not sufficiently robust

Experimental concerns: hyperparameters vary significantly across datasets (Table 7) suggesting sensitivity; no statistical significance tests provided; some improvements fall within standard deviation ranges

strengths: Novel perspective on continual learning: correcting catastrophic forgetting post-hoc via retrospector modules rather than preventing it during training represents an interesting and creative paradigm shift

Strong empirical results on S-CIFAR100 and S-TinyImg benchmarks, with RFE (no past data) outperforming several rehearsal-based baselines without accessing past task data—a practically valuable contribution
Practical integrability: method operates as post-training auxiliary modules with minimal disruption to standard training procedures, enabling easy adoption in existing ML pipelines

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three standard benchmarks with proper baselines (TAMiL, CLS-ER, ER-MKD), multiple runs with different seeds, detailed hyperparameter specifications, and helpful ablation studies
Effective visualizations (PCA in Figure 5) demonstrating rectification effectiveness; good presentation of core ideas with clear motivation and well-structured narrative
weaknesses: Weak generalization across datasets: RFE achieves only 91.15% on S-CIFAR10 vs. 94.99% for CLS-ER; authors acknowledge 'potential instability in rectifying fine-grained details' but provide no investigation, suggesting the method may not be broadly applicable

Poor class-incremental learning performance: RFE obtains 43.63% on S-CIFAR100 CIL vs. 50.68% baseline; the simple averaging strategy for task inference is ad-hoc and the CIL extension appears incomplete

Weak theoretical justification for core assumption: using current task data D_t^train to approximate D_{t-1} for training retrospectors (Eq. 2) lacks principled analysis of approximation quality or error bounds despite being central to the data-free RFE variant

Unvalidated invertibility assumption: method assumes feature drift can be meaningfully reversed, but analysis of recoverable information loss or how auxiliary feature extractor h_t actually compensates beyond empirical validation is missing; no error bounds for sequential chaining

Misleading claims about efficiency: Despite 'lightweight' characterization, retrospectors accumulate to 0.35M parameters each (23.76M training params vs. 11.17M for ER); inference slows 57% (7.36s→11.54s); marginal improvements on S-CIFAR100 (within error bars) vs. these overheads

Incomplete hyperparameter search: Table 4 shows α ∈ {1} with no actual sweep despite this being critical parameter in Eq. 7 weighting feature estimation loss; misleading claim of 'minimal changes to training' since Eq. 7 adds computational cost

Limited technical justification for architecture choices: soft gating + linear projections + auxiliary feature extractor design appears empirically driven; ablations show gating outperforms MLP baselines (52.78% vs 79.54%) but lack deeper analysis of why specific design is necessary

Error propagation in inference chains not analyzed: features pass through N-t_i retrospector modules sequentially with no error accumulation analysis; Figure 5 visualization uses 2D PCA (unrepresentative of 512D feature space)

strengths: Novel approach of using inference-time correction through chained retrospector modules to address catastrophic forgetting, separating forgetting mitigation from new task learning
Comprehensive experimental setup with multiple datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny ImageNet), strong baselines (ER, AGEM, DER++, CLS-ER, TAMiL), and detailed evaluation including TIL and CIL settings
Clear and honest limitations discussion acknowledging parameter overhead, inference cost, poor performance on S-CIFAR10, and task identity requirements
Good visualizations and analysis (PCA representations, forgetting matrices, RMSE measurements across task sequences)
Modular design enables integration into existing pipelines with minimal modifications to main training process
Detailed experimental setup, hyperparameter ranges, and reproducibility information in appendices
weaknesses: Core assumption that current task data D_t serves as valid proxy for D_{t-1} during retrospector training is not theoretically or empirically justified—why should feature drift from task t reflect the drift that occurred between tasks t-1 and t?

Inconsistent empirical results across benchmarks: significant underperformance on S-CIFAR10 (92.92% vs 96.02% for CLS-ER), comparable on S-CIFAR100, and improvement only on S-TinyImg; paper cherry-picks strongest results

Central 'data-free' advantage is undermined in practice: RFE without past data shows degradation over long sequences; practical variants (RFE-P, RFE-B) require storing past data anyway, negating primary claimed advantage over buffer-based methods
Severe weakness on class-incremental learning: RFE (43.63%) underperforms CLS-ER (56.18%) by 12.55% (Table 3); simple averaging strategy is admittedly suboptimal, limiting real-world applicability
Significant parameter overhead during training: 23.76M params vs 11.17M baseline (2.1x); inference time increases 57% (11.54s vs 7.36s), contradicting 'lightweight' characterization

Weak auxiliary feature extractor design contradicts itself: paper claims intentionally weak h_t to isolate retrospector effectiveness, but weak features cannot effectively recover forgotten information; circular reasoning without theoretical justification
Task identity requirement limits applicability: TIL requires provided task identity (unrealistic), and CIL relies on weak averaging strategy; extension to class-incremental learning is incomplete

Error propagation through long retrospector chains not analyzed: sequential application r_N ∘ ... ∘ r_{t+1} compounds approximation errors; while RMSE improves from ~1.3 to ~0.6, dynamics are not rigorously analyzed
Missing theoretical analysis: no justification for why inverse mapping learned from task t's feature drift generalizes to task t-1's original features; domain adaptation aspects not addressed

Confounded experimental comparisons: different baselines use different architectural components (CLS-ER uses 2 EMA backbones, TAMiL uses task-specific autoencoders); direct parameter-count comparison is problematic

strengths: Novel and genuinely different perspective on continual learning that decouples catastrophic forgetting mitigation from new task learning through retrospective feature mapping
Strong empirical results on S-CIFAR100 and S-TinyImg, significantly outperforming strong baselines (TAMiL, CLS-ER) with 79.54% vs 75.12% and 69.66% vs 63.28% respectively
Data-free RFE variant is competitive with rehearsal-based methods despite not accessing past task data—a notable achievement
Flexible framework with three principled variants (RFE, RFE-P, RFE-B) addressing different performance-privacy tradeoffs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple datasets, task settings, strong baselines, and extended analyses including 20-task sequences and ViT architectures
Excellent visualization and analysis with PCA visualizations clearly demonstrating feature rectification and RMSE quantification of effectiveness
Well-executed reproducibility with detailed hyperparameter search, training procedures, and promised code release
Minimal disruption to standard training process—modifications mainly post-training using auxiliary modules
weaknesses: Significant performance gap on S-CIFAR10 (91.15% vs 96.02% for CLS-ER), suggesting instability with fine-grained representations; paper attributes this to 'potential instability in rectifying fine-grained details' but doesn't resolve the issue
Weak class-incremental learning performance without task identity: RFE achieves 43.63% (vs 50.68% CLS-ER) on S-CIFAR100 and 26.59% (vs 20.25%) on S-TinyImg, with only simple averaging as solution
Linear parameter growth with number of tasks and inference cost scaling (Table 6: 11.54s vs 7.71s baseline)—fundamental scalability concerns for long task sequences not adequately addressed
Auxiliary feature extractor design appears ad-hoc and engineered for specific benchmarks; circular logic of using a network to compensate for catastrophic forgetting to solve catastrophic forgetting
Strong assumption that current task data D_t approximates D_t-1 for training retrospectors without theoretical justification or empirical validation of approximation quality
Lack of theoretical analysis for why mapping from t-domain to (t-1)-domain preserves discriminative information or characterization of when approach should work
Design choice justifications missing (e.g., why retrospector takes raw x as input in Eq. 3; why L2 distance in Eq. 2; limited ablation on gating mechanisms)
Task identity dependency limits flexibility compared to methods operating without task identity information
Retrospector error accumulation over long chains not analyzed—potential for errors to propagate through multiple mapping layers
Post-training design seems less critical than claimed, as Table 7 shows end-to-end training achieves similar performance (79.18% vs 79.54%)
